reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which first asked about AI use in September 2023, puts AI use in educational services (NAICS 61) at 30.0% in the latest period, down from 35.5% in the prior period. That is the only measured adoption figure in the material, and it covers firms answering yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks.

The federal government's own posture is set out by the Department of Education, which maintains an inventory of AI use-cases and frames its work around responsible and secure usage under the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. The use-cases it lists are operational rather than instructional: CAISY for real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation; Grammarly for written communication; Otter.AI for real-time transcription and collaboration in meetings, interviews, and lectures; and AWS Bedrock for building and scaling applications on foundation models. Others include generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in multiple programming languages, extracting key points and action items from public documents, generating mock data sets for testing, and training employees on prompt engineering. The Department also describes using fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information to test filters and data loss prevention.

On the supply side, HolonIQ describes itself as a platform for impact market intelligence, covering the global impact economy, and the sourced points describe it as tracking EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher education, and workforce learning. Its page text is about capability rather than findings: sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios, and mapping competitive landscapes for governments, institutions, technology companies, and investors. It reports no education-specific adoption or spending numbers in this material.

The course catalog on this site lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, with 3 carrying public companion code, each with one verified source and re-verified daily. Ten courses are tracked in the accompanying description, all offering free access to core materials, with three pairing that with a paid certificate option or public code repositories. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. The catalog notes that university courses tend to be structured around exam-driven theory while the industry courses are described as code-first or hands-on, and that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a narrow set of conclusions. The Census Bureau figure is the only measured adoption number, and it moved down between the two periods reported. The Department of Education's inventory shows what a large education-adjacent institution actually runs, which is drafting, transcription, summarization, code assistance, and testing of data loss prevention rather than student-facing tutoring. The market-intelligence and course-catalog sources describe what is available and how it is organized, not what it returns. None of the sources here report ROI evidence for education deployments, and none report regulatory enforcement specific to the sector beyond the Department's stated adherence to federal AI regulations and the executive order.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
